query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase FCC high‐entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the main constituents, adding a small, controlled amount (around 0.5 wt%) of Y2O3 nanoparticles during powder processing will refine and stabilize the microstructure at high temperatures. This nanoparticle dispersion is expected to inhibit grain growth during elevated-temperature service and thereby yield an alloy with markedly improved yield strength and creep resistance compared to the same alloy processed without nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: A titanium– and nickel–containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase, FCC solid solution state (with Ti and Ni as primary constituents).
generation.intervention: Introduce ~0.5 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles by a powder surface modification (e.g., via resonant acoustic mixing) before consolidation (e.g., by direct energy deposition or a similar additive manufacturing method).
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature testing conditions, such as tensile or creep tests performed between 800 °C and 1000 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined grain structure with nanoparticles located at grain boundaries acting as pinning centers.
generation.mechanism: The dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles impede grain boundary migration and coarsening during high-temperature exposure. They create a stable microstructure that hinders dislocation motion and improves load distribution, resulting in enhanced solid solution and grain boundary strengthening under elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a nanoparticle-free alloy, the nanoparticle-enhanced alloy is predicted to exhibit a significant improvement—on the order of 15–30% higher yield strength and better creep resistance—at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The same Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy processed without nanoparticle incorporation, which typically shows coarser grains and lower high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable to FCC high-entropy alloys with titanium and nickel as major components, processed under additive manufacturing conditions (e.g., DED), and evaluated under high-temperature regimes (approximately 800–1000 °C). The effect may be composition and process sensitive and may not extend to alloys with different dominant phases or processing routes.
generation.uncertainty: While similar benefits of Y2O3 nanoparticles—such as grain refinement and improved high-temperature properties—have been demonstrated in NiCoCr-based and dispersion-strengthened multi-principal element alloys (e.g., evidence in PMC10222657 and PMC7296023), the precise magnitude of improvement and long-term phase stability in a Ti–Ni dominant alloy remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the target high-entropy alloy using the same processing route: one with the addition of ~0.5 wt% Y2O3 nanoparticles (via acoustic mixing prior to deposition) and one without. Fabricate samples using an additive manufacturing method such as DED under identical parameters. After processing, subject both sets to post-deposition heat treatment (if applicable) to ensure homogenization. Characterize the microstructure via SEM/EBSD to measure grain size distributions and nanoparticle dispersion. Then perform high-temperature tensile tests and creep tests in the 800–1000 °C range.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase homogeneity (using SEM/EBSD, XRD)
Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at high temperature
Creep rupture life and strain rate under controlled stress at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticle‐enhanced alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (i.e., less than approximately 15% increase in yield strength and creep resistance) over the control alloy, or if the microstructural analysis does not reveal a refined grain structure with effective nanoparticle pinning, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
